rows.notes: The cited study is a literature review (self-described 'Review Article' and 'literature survey study') on agricultural water management in Tanzania; it reports no own data. It only mentions drip irrigation once, noting that drip and sprinklers demand high initial capital (citing [76]); it reports no water-use-efficiency figures for drip, let alone 40-70%.

Review article with no primary data. It contains no result on yields under drip irrigation; the only yield-related remark on modern irrigation is a general statement citing [53] that positive yield responses have been realized where modern irrigation approaches were adopted.

Review article with no primary data. Nothing in the study addresses drip irrigation maintaining yields under drought; drought adaptation discussed concerns drought-resistant crops, mulching, water harvesting and agroforestry, all cited from other work.

Review article with no primary data. The study says nothing about drip irrigation precision, nutrient distribution or soil health effects of drip; the only soil-related irrigation remark is that over-irrigation causes salt accumulation and nutrient leaching (citing [70]).

notes: The document is a narrative literature review (Advances in Meteorology, 'Review Article') on water use in Tanzanian smallholder agriculture. It presents no own experiment, survey or model; Figure 1 reproduces FAO statistics and Figure 2 is a sketch. Drip irrigation is mentioned only as a high-capital technology. None of the four claims (smart drip WUE gains of 40-70%, stable yields under drought, uniform nutrient distribution/soil health) is supported by this source; the citation appears misattributed.
